Pet odor outlasts cleaning because of what it's made of. Urine leaves uric acid crystals that bond to fibers and foam; general "pet smell" is oils and dander ground into fabric over years. Neither dissolves in soap and water — which is why the couch smells fine after cleaning, then announces itself again on the first humid day as crystals reactivate.

Two things actually work: **enzyme cleaners**, which digest the odor compounds rather than covering them, and **removal of what's saturated**. Everything below is one of those two.

## Sofas: The Treatment Sequence

**Find every source first.** Your nose adapts; a UV flashlight in a dark room doesn't — urine fluoresces. Treating the spot you know about while missing two others is the most common reason "I already tried enzyme cleaner" fails.

**Fresh accidents: extract before treating.** Blot straight down with pressure until towels come away nearly dry. Everything you lift now never reaches the foam.

**Apply enzyme cleaner correctly — this is where results are won or lost.** The enzyme needs to reach everywhere the urine reached, which means saturating the spot more generously than instinct suggests, then staying wet for its full dwell time (often 10–15 minutes minimum; some label directions run longer). Check the care tag first — W or W/S codes only — and test a hidden spot.

**Dry thoroughly, assess honestly, repeat once.** A second treatment resolves a surprising share of survivors. A smell that outlasts two full treatments is coming from deep foam.

**For general pet-musk without accidents:** HEPA-vacuum thoroughly, hot-wash removable covers, baking soda overnight, vacuum again. That sequence plus the [dander-control routine](/blog/home-cleaning/pet-allergies-and-couches-cleaning-vs-replacing/) handles odor and allergen together.

## Rugs: Easier, With One Trap

Rugs are more treatable than sofas — the fibers are the whole story, no foam core. Same sequence: locate, extract, saturate with enzyme cleaner, full dwell, dry flat. The trap is the **backing and the pad underneath**: a soaked-through accident means treating the rug's underside and the pad too, or replacing the pad — pads are cheap, and a clean rug over a contaminated pad still smells. Machine-washable rugs: hot wash with an enzyme additive beats all spot treatment.

## When the Odor Has Won

Replace rather than keep fighting when: smells return after two full enzyme treatments; the couch had years of accidents or a long-term marking problem; odor rises when you press cushions (that's the foam exhaling); or warm weather reliably revives it. Trapped odor compounds also mean the couch [fails donation inspection](/blog/eco-friendly-living/can-couch-be-donated/) automatically — so the realistic path is [removal](/couch-removal/), and choosing [a less absorbent material](/blog/home-cleaning/best-worst-couch-materials-for-allergies/) for its successor.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What neutralizes pet odor permanently?

Enzyme cleaners are the only consumer product that destroys odor compounds rather than masking them. Baking soda helps surface smell; vinegar helps mild cases; nothing in a scented spray removes anything.

### Why does my couch smell like dog even after washing the covers?

Because the odor source is below the covers — oils and dander in the body fabric and foam. Covers are the washable layer; the couch underneath accumulated the same years of contact without ever being laundered.

### Does baking soda really remove pet smells?

It absorbs surface odor genuinely but temporarily — good maintenance, not treatment. For anything urine-based, only enzymatic cleaning addresses the source.

### When should I give up on a pet-odor couch?

After two correct, full-dwell enzyme treatments fail, the compounds are in foam you can't reach. Continuing to treat the surface is paying rent on a problem that isn't moving out — [pricing a replacement pickup](/pricing/) is usually the better spend.
